tier_reason: The README 'How fast' section claims '1.2x-50x faster' than CPython 3.12 on four named workloads and 'about on par' on fib(30), but gives no per-benchmark times, no CPU, no compiler or flags; the scripts it says are in tests/ do not exist there (tests/ holds only correctness tests and compare_python.sh, tools/ only gen_stdlib.sh). First-party range with no methodology is C at best.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile default is $(CC) with CFLAGS ?= -O2 plus -std=gnu11 (built with clang on Termux per the README); the compiler, version and flags used for the README timings are not stated
corrections.workload: README 'How fast' section names a numeric loop, building a list, filling and reading a dict, a hot attribute-access loop and a recursive fib(30). The README says 'see tests/ for the exact scripts', but tests/ contains only the correctness tests t01-t12 and t90 (.cpy plus expected .out) and compare_python.sh, so the benchmark programs are not published.
corrections.caveats: Brand-new repository (all six commits dated 2026-09-22, 0 stars, 0 forks). The README gives only a 1.2x-50x range with no per-benchmark numbers, no compiler or flags and no CPU; the benchmark scripts it points to ('see tests/') are not in the repository, and tests/compare_python.sh only diffs program output against CPython 3.12, so the ratios cannot be reproduced. Semantics differ from CPython in ways that help numeric loops: int is 64-bit and raises OverflowError instead of promoting to bigint, memory is reference-counted only (reference cycles are never collected), and there is no bytes/bytearray, complex, match, async/await or __slots__. It is a tree-walking AST interpreter (no bytecode); generators each run on their own OS thread with an 8 MB stack, so generator-heavy code is likely slow. Low confidence.

notes: Claim text in the record matches the README; the only real fix is that the 'exact scripts' the README cites do not exist in tests/ or tools/, so there is no benchmark code at all. Kept at C as a weak first-party range claim (one could argue D since no individual number is given); flag 0 stars, one-day-old repo, int64-only ints and no cycle collection. MIT licence (LICENSE file, 2026 moonlite-admin) and last commit 2026-09-22 confirmed.

corrections.caveats: First-party micro-benchmarks (fib(30), a 1M-iteration counting loop, tail calls) on one unnamed Windows x86_64 machine; each script times a single run in-process (newLISP (time ...) or time-of-day, Python time.perf_counter after a small warmup), no repeats or variance. The 17.3 ms 'tail-recursive loop' row compares a different program shape against CPython's while loop, and the TCO table (100M self-tail steps in 1,023 ms, 10M mutual steps in 167 ms) has no baseline time because CPython raises RecursionError. The CPython 3.12.3 to 3.14.4 gap on fib(30) (186.9 ms vs 86.0 ms, 2.17x) is larger than usual, which suggests differently built interpreters; their provenance is not stated. All VM work landed 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-17 (earliest commit 2024-10-19 is the upstream import); constructs the bytecode VM cannot compile fall back to the original tree-walker. GPL-3.0 (documentation GFDL). Forks irr/newlisp-spark and irr/newlisp-neo-fork were not opened.

notes: All README numbers match the record (fib 42.6 vs 86.0 ms = 2.02x, loop 31.3 vs 37.2 ms = 1.19x, TCO loop 17.3 ms). Dev run used pyccel commit 0ccf9ec3e964e071b933947b75767a052c9692f4, numba 0.66.0, pythran 0.18.1, numpy 2.4.6 (version_specific_results/devel_performance_312_requirements.txt)

corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the Pyccel developers' own benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks, 5 stars), regenerated by a GitHub Actions workflow on an ubuntu-latest shared runner; CPU model and compiler versions are not stated. Execution times are python3 -m timeit best-of results and exclude compilation; the compile-time table is CPU seconds (rusage user plus system) and lists 0.33 to 8.31 s per kernel across all tools. The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples, so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. Pyccel is not the fastest accelerator in its own table: the GNU C backend is slower than Pythran (GNU) on 6 of 12 shared kernels (Dijkstra, FD L Convection, FD NL Convection, FD Poisson, FD Laplace, M-D), and the GNU Fortran backend is slower than Pythran on Dijkstra and M-D. Built with -ffast-math. Pyccel is an ahead-of-time Python-to-C/Fortran transpiler (filed next to Cython, Codon and Nuitka), not an interpreter. The JOSS paper was not opened (host blocked), so no peer-reviewed numbers are used.

notes: Every number in the record matches the dev-branch table; added the four missing kernels, the Fortran-backend ratios and the run details from the workflow (Python 3.12 confirmed, not just inferred; ubuntu-latest runner). Corrected the caveat that Pyccel trails Pythran on only three kernels: the C backend trails it on six.
